assignments.title: Critical Questions: The Journals of Lewis and Clark
assignments.html:
MODULE 1 · CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Critical Questions: The Journals of Lewis and Clark
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
≈ ≈ ≈
Instructions

Read the primary source for this week: selections from the Journals of Lewis and Clark. Then answer both questions in your own words. Aim for four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. Suppose the Mandan and the Nez Perce had refused to help the explorers during the hard winter months. What might have happened to the expedition, and to Jefferson's hopes for the new land?
  2. Using the journals and the lesson The New Republic Competes with Colonial Powers in North America, explain how the purchase of Louisiana in 1803 led to this journey.

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

assignments.title: Primary Source Exercise: The Monroe Doctrine (1823)
assignments.html:
MODULE 1 · PRIMARY SOURCE EXERCISE
Primary Source Exercise: The Monroe Doctrine (1823)
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
≈ ≈ ≈
Instructions

Read the primary source: President Monroe's Annual Message to Congress of 1823. Then answer both questions in your own words, in four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. What events in Latin America and in Europe led Monroe to send this message in 1823?
  2. Suppose Britain had not wanted free trade and had not backed Monroe's message with its navy. How might the powers of Europe have reacted to his warning, and why?

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

assignments.title: Critical Questions: Clay's Defense of the American System (1832)
assignments.html:
MODULE 1 · CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Critical Questions: Clay's Defense of the American System (1832)
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
≈ ≈ ≈
Instructions

Read the primary source for this week: Henry Clay's speech in defense of the American System. Then answer both questions in your own words. Aim for four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. Clay argues that his plan would help every region. Using the speech and the lesson Clay Proposes the American System to Strengthen the Nation, explain what caused many Southerners to disagree with him even though he promised benefits for all.
  2. Clay's idea of a "home market" rests on a belief about what makes a country strong and free. Name that belief in your own words, and explain how it connects to the lesson's point that a nation which depends on others for its tools and cloth is not truly free.

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

assignments.title: Primary Source Exercise: Jackson on Indian Removal (1830)
assignments.html:
MODULE 1 · PRIMARY SOURCE EXERCISE
Primary Source Exercise: Jackson on Indian Removal (1830)
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
≈ ≈ ≈
Instructions

Read the primary source: President Jackson's Second Annual Message of 1830, the part about Indian removal. Then answer both questions in your own words, in four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. Jackson says removal will help both settlers and Native nations. Using the message and the lesson Jackson Presides over Democracy in America, explain what pressures led him to support removal.
  2. Jackson spoke as a President who believed he stood for "the people." Explain how that idea of democracy could include white farmers and still leave out the Cherokee. What does this show about who counted as "the people"?

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

quizzes.title: Intro (Lessons 1.1 and 1.2): How Do Outside Powers Shape a Young Nation?
quizzes.description:
MODULE 1 · INTRO QUIZ
Module 1 Intro: How Do Outside Powers Shape a Young Nation?
3 questions · survey · one attempt
≈ ≈ ≈
Before you start

Before you start these lessons, answer three quick questions. There are no wrong answers. You will come back to the first question when you finish.

Start with The New Republic Competes with Colonial Powers in North America.

questions.text: A young country shares a continent with older, stronger countries. How might wars and revolutions far away change what that young country does? Answer in two or three sentences. You will revisit this answer at the end of these lessons.
I have read the goals for these lessons: to explain how the Louisiana Purchase, the War of 1812, and the Monroe Doctrine changed the place of the United States in North America.

answers.text: Yes, I am ready to begin
Not yet, I have a question

questions.text: This quarter has an optional group capstone. Would you like to work in a group?

answers.text: Yes
No, I will work on my own

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: Lessons 1.1 and 1.2
quizzes.description:
MODULE 1 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: The New Republic Competes with Colonial Powers in North America and Madison Wars with Britain; Monroe Warns Europe to Stay Out of the Western Hemisphere
7 questions · 7 points · 2 attempts
≈ ≈ ≈
Before you start

This quiz covers The New Republic Competes with Colonial Powers in North America and Madison Wars with Britain; Monroe Warns Europe to Stay Out of the Western Hemisphere. You may take it twice, and your higher score counts. Some questions ask you to put two or more facts together, so think before you answer.

questions.text: Napoleon first wanted Louisiana as a supply base for a sugar colony, yet in 1803 he offered to sell all of it. Which explanation fits the facts best?

answers.text: The revolution in Saint-Domingue defeated his army, so Louisiana had little value to him, and he needed money for war against Britain.
Spain demanded Louisiana back and France could not refuse.
Jefferson threatened to invade New Orleans unless France sold the land.
Toussaint Louverture offered to pay France for the territory.

questions.text: Jefferson worried about whether buying Louisiana was allowed. Which of his earlier beliefs explains that worry?

answers.text: He believed the Senate should never approve treaties.
He believed the United States should never own land west of the Mississippi.
He believed the President had no role in dealing with France.
He believed the federal government could use only the powers the Constitution lists.

questions.text: The Embargo Act of 1807 failed to change British or French behavior. Which fact best explains why?

answers.text: Congress passed it only a few days before the war began.
Britain and France found other places to buy goods, while American sailors, merchants, and farmers bore the cost.
French ships were not affected, but British ships stopped trading entirely.
Jefferson ended the embargo within a week.

questions.text: Which conclusion about the Lewis and Clark expedition does the lesson best support?

answers.text: It reached the Pacific mainly because Lewis and Clark carried supplies for the whole trip.
It showed that a water route to the Pacific was easy to find.
It depended on Native nations for food, horses, and directions, and on people like Sacagawea.
It was carried out without any contact with Native nations.

questions.text: How did the War of 1812 change the position of Native nations in the Northwest?

answers.text: They gained new allies and held their land more firmly.
They were given their own state by the Treaty of Ghent.
They lost Tecumseh and British help, and settlers moved in faster than before.
They agreed to sell their land to Britain.

questions.text: Spain gave Florida to the United States in the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819. Which event most clearly showed that Spain could not defend Florida?

answers.text: The burning of Washington in 1814.
The Embargo Act of 1807.
Tecumseh's death in 1813.
Jackson's 1818 invasion, when he seized Spanish forts.

questions.text: The Monroe Doctrine was a bold claim from a country that could not enforce it. What really stood behind it?

answers.text: The American army, which was now the largest in the world.
The British navy, because Britain wanted free trade in the Americas and did not want other empires there.
A treaty with Spain that closed Latin America to Europe.
A promise from Napoleon to stay out of the hemisphere.

quizzes.title: Outro (Lessons 1.1 and 1.2): Looking Back at a Nation Among Powers
quizzes.description:
MODULE 1 · OUTRO QUIZ
Module 1 Outro: Looking Back at a Nation Among Powers
4 questions · survey · one attempt
≈ ≈ ≈
Before you start

You have finished these lessons and their work. Answer four short questions. Your answers help your teacher see where students feel strong and where more help is needed.

questions.text: At the start you answered this question: how might wars and revolutions far away change what a young country does? Answer it again now in two or three sentences. If your answer changed, say what changed it.
How confident do you feel explaining why the United States was able to buy Louisiana in 1803?

answers.text: 1 - Not at all confident
2 - A little confident
3 - Somewhat confident
4 - Mostly confident
5 - Very confident

questions.text: Which idea from these lessons is still unclear to you? It might be the Louisiana Purchase, impressment, Tecumseh's confederacy, the Adams-Onis Treaty, or the Monroe Doctrine. Say what you do not yet understand.

Lewis and Clark's party crossed the continent through hard winters and unknown country. Which of these virtues did that journey require: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, or responsibility? Explain in two or three sentences, and tell about a time you needed that same virtue.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: Lessons 1.3 and 1.4
quizzes.description:
MODULE 1 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: Clay Proposes the American System to Strengthen the Nation and Jackson Presides over Democracy in America
7 questions · 7 points · 2 attempts
≈ ≈ ≈
Before you start

This quiz covers Clay Proposes the American System to Strengthen the Nation and Jackson Presides over Democracy in America. You may take it twice, and your higher score counts. Some questions ask you to put two or more facts together, so think before you answer.

questions.text: Clay said his American System would help every region, yet many Southerners opposed the protective tariff. Which fact best explains their view?

answers.text: Southern planters owned most of the factories that the tariff protected.
Southern states had no ports and could not import goods.
Planters sold cotton to Britain and bought many goods from abroad, so a tariff raised their costs and might reduce British buying.
The tariff had been passed without a vote in Congress.

questions.text: Clay's "home market" idea depended on each region needing the others. Which description matches the plan?

answers.text: Northern factories made goods, while Southern planters and Western farmers sold cotton and food to Northern workers.
Southern factories made goods for Western farmers, who sold them to the North.
Each region would trade only with foreign countries.
The Northern states would grow cotton and the Southern states would build the canals.

questions.text: Madison vetoed the 1817 bill for roads and canals because he doubted the Constitution allowed it. Which earlier argument does his veto remind you of?

answers.text: The argument over whether to count slaves in the census.
The argument over whether the Supreme Court should have nine justices.
The argument over whether to move the capital to the Potomac.
The argument between Hamilton and Jefferson over whether Congress may use powers that are not listed.

questions.text: In 1824 Andrew Jackson won the most electoral and popular votes, yet John Quincy Adams became President. What was the reason?

answers.text: Jackson refused to take the oath of office.
No candidate won a majority of electors, so the House of Representatives decided.
The Supreme Court ruled that Jackson was not eligible.
Adams won more popular votes in the Western states.

questions.text: Which statement about the right to vote in Jackson's time is best supported by the lesson?

answers.text: The vote widened for white men, while some free Black men lost the right to vote.
Women gained the vote in the new Western states.
Property rules for voting were made stricter in every state.
Native Americans gained the vote when they moved west.

questions.text: In Worcester v. Georgia the Supreme Court said Georgia had no right to rule Cherokee land, yet the Cherokee were still removed. Why did the ruling fail to protect them?

answers.text: The Court reversed itself the next year.
The Cherokee asked to be removed.
Georgia ignored the ruling, and Jackson did nothing to enforce it.
Congress passed a law canceling the decision.

questions.text: Many Black Seminoles fought beside the Seminoles in the Second Seminole War. What is the best explanation?

answers.text: They had been promised land by the United States Army.
They would likely lose their freedom if the army won.
They were forced to fight by Seminole leaders.
They wanted to move west of the Mississippi.

discussions.title: Discussion: Tecumseh's Confederacy and the Road to the War of 1812
discussions.html:
MODULE 1 · DISCUSSION
Discussion: Tecumseh's Confederacy and the Road to the War of 1812
10 points · written post and one reply · threaded discussion
≈ ≈ ≈
The prompt

Historians disagree about what pushed the United States into war in 1812. Some stress British seizure of American sailors at sea. Others stress trouble on the frontier, where Tecumseh and the Native confederacy were seen as a threat backed by Britain. Make one specific claim about which cause mattered more, or whether the two were really one story. Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Was Jackson's Election a Triumph for Democracy?
discussions.html:
MODULE 1 · DISCUSSION
Discussion: Was Jackson's Election a Triumph for Democracy?
10 points · written post and one reply · threaded discussion
≈ ≈ ≈
The prompt

Jackson's election in 1828 brought far more voters to the polls and made the presidency a voice for ordinary men. His years in office also saw Indian removal and the loss of the vote for some free Black men. Make one specific claim: was Jackson's election a triumph for democracy, a mixed result, or something else? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.
